gist: Atwood closes the Poemander testimony of illumination and argues that the 'operative revelation of Intellect' is known only by experience, that the First Principle is reached only by a theurgically prepared seeker, and that Scripture and the Law veil a hidden Soul. She then presents the practical work through Synesius (gentle coction of one Water, all operations being one), Bacon's Proteus, the Matter as Isis bringing forth Orus, and two Rosicrucian speeches of the Matter (the Goddess with the five gates, the Dragon called Mercury), and ends with a call to real faith as the leader of experimental inquiry.

notes.point: Poemander withdraws. The narrator, taught the nature of the Whole, preaches piety and knowledge: bodily sleep was the mind's watchfulness, shut eyes true Sight, silence 'great with child'. Inspired with Truth, he ends in a hymn to the Father, 'To be praised in silence'.
notes.voice: QUOTED: The Divine Poemander of Hermes Trismegistus (the narrator Poemander spoke to)

notes.point: Nothing can make this operative revelation of Intellect more credible to the uninitiated. Those who cannot imagine disbelieve without experience; those with inner evidence will believe and know before observation forces the many to a faith which is blessed only in the Intuition.

Whoever seeks the First Principle must be theurgically prepared and pass corrosive and fiery ordeals, to rise to what is most united in nature, its Flower, through which it is Deity and binds the Universe in sympathetic consent.

Those to whom the Word came are called gods (John). Unbelief arises in ignorance: none looks 'under the Bark of the Law' (Agrippa). The veil over reading Moses lifts on turning to the Lord, who is Spirit; beholders are changed from glory to glory (the Apostle).

The Kabalist: each word of the Law cloaks a mystery; its story is its vestment; the wise seek its Soul, the Law itself. Atwood: without it nothing is truly known. Paul: the Fathers drank of a spiritual rock, 'and that rock was Christ'.
notes.voice: QUOTED: the Kabalist (endorsed by ATWOOD); St. Paul

notes.point: Synesius: labour only for the Water that blackens, dissolves, congeals, putrefies and germinates. Decoct it gently and long until its false tincture becomes light; don't burn its flowers or hasten; shut the vessel. All named operations are one decoction of nature; extracting soul, spirit or body is calcination, the 'operation of Venus'.

The soul is extracted and reduced upon the body until the four elements commix. Two luminaries appear, fixed male below, volatile above; when the lower rises upon the upper, an incomparable Luminary issues.
This was the Experiment that led 'our Fathers' into Experience and illumination; theirs was the true philosophy, its end Christian regeneration.

It is the Art of Democritus in Bacon's Proteus: matter forced toward annihilation runs through all shapes and restores itself if force continues; binding it in the extremest degrees works best. Atwood: that is, life's last exigence, before rebirth by the recreative Light within.

Then the Matter is Isis, the Divine I Am, Myrionymous, able to take any Form the Supreme Reason impresses. In herself Nothing, pre-existent mother of all, miraculous; by the Fire of nature she brings forth Orus, the Philosophic Sun.

A Rosy Cross Goddess pours milk and blood to be boiled into silver and gold; poison named the flying eagle, she is the First Matter, hidden from the wicked. Eagle's tears and Lion's blood combined are the treasure; the pair become a Salamander curing men and metals.
notes.voice: QUOTED: fraternity of the Rosy Cross

notes.point: Five gates: knowledge of the matter; preparation (water, blood, a spiritual bright body); fire to maturity; multiplication by weights; projection. The fourth gives a universal medicine, the fifth serves only metals. The mystery, God's Word breathed into nature, is given to few though seen daily.
notes.voice: QUOTED: fraternity of the Rosy Cross

notes.point: The Dragon: everywhere and free; its water and fire dissolve and compound; unknown, it destroys the senses; separate thick from thin, with courage. It is the Egg of nature, Mercury wedded to Gold philosophical, all contraries, the Light of nature within, transmuting base metals.
notes.voice: QUOTED: fraternity of the Rosy Cross

notes.point: Atwood: nourish even a small real faith until experience rewards it; without faith and the ideal conception nothing is proven. It is not credulity but self-evidencing liberty of thought, revealing Nature's occult Causality; the right-believer will not be deceived.

method.veiled: For the sleep of the body was the sober watchfulness of the mind; and the shutting of my eyes the true Sight; and my silence great with child and full of good
method.plain: In the state of illumination the body sleeps and the eyes are shut while the mind is fully awake and sees truly; the inner silence is fertile.
method.basis: III.3 ¶58 sets bodily sleep against mental watchfulness and shut eyes against 'true Sight'; Atwood calls this testimony the 'operative revelation of Intellect' with 'experimental knowledge' (III.3 ¶59).
method.voice: QUOTED: The Divine Poemander of Hermes Trismegistus (endorsed by ATWOOD)

also.text: whereby I became inspired by God with the Truth
To be praised in silence.

method.veiled: operative revelation of Intellect
method.plain: Atwood treats the Poemander account as testimony to a real, working revelation of Intellect, known experimentally; it cannot be made credible to those without the experience.
method.basis: III.3 ¶59: 'or its experimental knowledge more credible to the uninitiated'; 'They who cannot imagine will disbelieve without experience'.

also.text: They who cannot imagine will disbelieve without experience

method.veiled: he must be theurgically prepared, and pass through many preliminary ordeals, corrosive tests, and fiery solutions and dissolutions refining
method.plain: Whoever seeks the First Principle must himself be prepared and undergo refining trials described in chemical terms (corrosion, solution, dissolution); in this sentence it is the seeker who is refined and raised.
method.basis: III.3 ¶59: the grammatical subject is the person ('he must be ... prepared'), and the purpose is 'in order to raise himself'. 'Theurgically' is not defined in this chunk.

method.veiled: That which is the most united in nature, and to its Flower, and That through which it is Deity
method.plain: The goal is the First Principle: the most unified point of nature, its highest flowering, by which nature is divine; it hangs from its own source and holds the Universe in sympathy with itself.
method.basis: III.3 ¶59 continues: 'by which it is suspended from its proper fountain, and connects and causes the Universe to have a sympathetic consent with Itself'.

method.veiled: when Moses is read, the veil is upon their heart
method.plain: Unbelief comes from ignorance of Scripture's hidden sense: readers stop at the surface. The veil is taken away when the heart turns to the Lord.
method.basis: III.3 ¶59: 'Does not all our unbelief, as the common faith, arise in ignorance? For at present there is no profound understanding of the Scriptures'; 'the veil shall be taken away'.

also.text: nor does any look, as Agrippa says, under the Bark of the Law
when it shall turn to the Lord, says the Apostle, the veil shall be taken away

method.veiled: are changed into the same image from glory to glory, even as by the Spirit of the Lord
method.plain: With the veil removed, those who behold the Lord's glory as in a glass are transformed into that same image, by the Spirit. The chunk does not explicitly tie this to the work beyond placing it in Atwood's argument.
method.basis: III.3 ¶59 says this directly; 'For the Lord is that Spirit'.

also.text: For the Lord is that Spirit, and where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is liberty.

method.veiled: The story of the Law is the vestment of the Law; unhappy he, who mistakes the vestment for the Law itself.
method.plain: Sacred texts must be read for their hidden sense: the literal narrative is a garment; every word hides a mystery; the real Law is its Soul, which the wise contemplate. Atwood adds that nothing is truly known without this Soul.
method.basis: III.3 ¶59: 'each word of the Law has a meaning and cloaks a mystery entirely sublime'; 'the Soul, which is the basis of all rest; which is the Law itself'; Atwood: 'Without which nothing is truly known; whose Experience is All.'

also.text: so that they may be prepared at length to contemplate and know that Soul which breathes in the Law
Without which nothing is truly known; whose Experience is All.

method.veiled: labour only for that Water which burns to blackness, dissolves and congeals
method.plain: The whole work is on one 'Water', to the exclusion of all else. Its stated properties: it blackens, dissolves, congeals, putrefies and causes germination. The chunk does not identify it further.
method.basis: III.3 ¶60: 'make no account of other things'; 'It is that which putrefies and causes germination'; no identification given.

also.text: It is that which putrefies and causes germination

method.veiled: Decoct it gently by little and little, until it have changed its false tincture into a perfect form of light
method.plain: Cook the Water gently and gradually over a long time, not grudging the time, until its false colouring becomes a perfect form of light.
method.basis: III.3 ¶60: 'wholly employ thyself in the coction of this water, and demur not at the expense of time; otherwise thou shalt gain no advantage'. Reading 'decoct' as gentle heating is ours; the text gives only 'gently by little and little'.

also.text: wholly employ thyself in the coction of this water, and demur not at the expense of time

method.veiled: have great care at the beginning, that thou burn not its flowers and its vivacity, and make not too much haste to come to an end of thy work
method.plain: Excess at the start destroys the matter's living quality ('flowers', 'vivacity'); haste to finish spoils the work.
method.basis: III.3 ¶60: the warning follows the instruction to decoct 'gently by little and little'.

method.veiled: Shut thy vessel well that it may not breathe out, so that thou mayest bring it to some effect
method.plain: Keep the vessel sealed so nothing escapes; otherwise no effect follows. This chunk does not say what the vessel is.
method.basis: III.3 ¶60; no gloss of 'vessel' in this chunk (n42 cites Eirenaeus and Norton for this sentence).

method.veiled: to dissolve, to calcine, to tinge, to whiten, to renew, to bathe, to wash, to coagulate, to imbibe, to decoct, to fix, to grind, to dry and to distill are all one
method.plain: The many operation names in the books are not separate procedures: all name one continuous operation, cooking nature until she is perfected.
method.basis: III.3 ¶60: they 'signify no more than to decoct nature until such time as she be perfected'. The sentence is introduced by 'and not that', likely a misprint for 'note' (see ambiguities).

also.text: signify no more than to decoct nature until such time as she be perfected

method.veiled: to extract the soul, or the spirit, or the body, is nothing else than the aforesaid calcinations in regard they signify the operation of Venus
method.plain: 'Extracting' soul, spirit or body is the same as the calcinations already named, which signify the 'operation of Venus'; through the fire of this extraction the spirit comes forth gently. This chunk does not explain 'Venus'.
method.basis: III.3 ¶60, direct equation ('is nothing else than'); 'operation of Venus' is not glossed.

also.text: It is through the fire of the extraction of the soul that the spirit comes forth gently

method.veiled: the extraction of the soul out of the body, and the reduction of it afterwards upon the same body; until the whole be drawn to a commixion of the four elements
method.plain: The soul is drawn out of the body and afterwards returned onto the same body, until the whole is brought to a mixture of all four elements.
method.basis: III.3 ¶60 directly.

method.veiled: there are made manifest two luminaries, the one fixed, the other not; whereof the fixed which is the male remains below, and the volatile remains above, moving itself perpetually
method.plain: Two lights appear: a fixed, male one below and a volatile, ever-moving one above. When the lower rises upon the upper and all is 'substantiated', a single incomparable Luminary issues. The chunk does not identify the luminaries further.
method.basis: III.3 ¶60 gives the sequence; it follows 'so that which is below, being like that which is above'.

also.text: until that which is below rises upon that which is above, and all being substantiated, there then issues forth an incomparable Luminary

method.veiled: That was the Experiment that led our Fathers into Experience, and illumination in the Divine Antecedent of all life.
method.plain: Atwood identifies the work just described as the experiment by which the ancients reached direct experience and illumination in the divine source of life; its worthiest end is Christian regeneration.
method.basis: III.3 ¶61: 'then was not theirs the right and true philosophy with Christian regeneration for its most worthy end?'

also.text: with Christian regeneration for its most worthy end

method.veiled: if any skillful minister of nature shall apply force to matter, and by design torture and vex it in order to its annihilation
method.plain: Matter deliberately constrained and pushed toward annihilation passes through every shape and, if the force is kept up, completes the cycle and restores itself. Binding it hard ('manacles and fetters') is most effective. Atwood calls this the Art of Democritus.
method.basis: III.3 ¶61: 'running through the whole circle of transformations and completing its period, it restores itself, if the force be continued'.

also.text: running through the whole circle of transformations and completing its period, it restores itself, if the force be continued
And that method of binding, torturing, and detaining will prove the most effectual and expeditious which makes use of manacles and fetters

method.veiled: lays hold of and works upon matter in the extremest degrees
method.plain: Atwood glosses 'extremest degrees' as the last extremity of life, when it is about to be reborn out of oblivion and defilement, drawn by the re-creating Light within.
method.basis: III.3 ¶61, Atwood's own gloss beginning 'That is'.

also.text: That is, in the last exigence of life; when it is about to be born again from out the oblivion of this worked and its defilements, by attraction of the recreative Light within.

method.veiled: Then she is Isis, the Divine I Am, by the Greeks called Myrionymous, or the goddess with a thousand names
method.plain: At this point the Matter is called Isis; her thousand names signify that it can understand and be converted into any form the Supreme Reason impresses on it.
method.basis: III.3 ¶62: 'hereby to denote the capacity with which such a Matter is endowed of understanding, and of being converted to all or any of the Forms or degrees of specific Law, which it may please the Supreme Reason to impress upon her'.

also.text: hereby to denote the capacity with which such a Matter is endowed of understanding, and of being converted to all or any of the Forms or degrees of specific Law

method.veiled: As respects herself, she is Nothing
method.plain: In herself the Matter is no particular thing, not animal, vegetable or mineral apart, but prior to all and mother of all; her birth and complexion are singular and miraculous.
method.basis: III.3 ¶62: 'neither animal nor vegetable nor mineral apart; but, --- pre-existent to them all, --- she is the mother of all'.

also.text: her birth, according to the Adepts, is singular and not without a miracle
I am well known and yet a mere nothing

method.veiled: that which she brings forth by the Fire of nature lawfully conceived, is Orus, the Philosophic Sun
method.plain: What the Matter brings forth by the 'Fire of nature', lawfully conceived, is called Orus, the Philosophic Sun. The chunk does not further explain the Fire of nature.
method.basis: III.3 ¶62, direct identification.

method.veiled: Though at the first sight thou art poison adorned with the name of the flying eagle; thou are the First Matter: the Seed of Divine benediction, in whose body there is heat and rain
method.plain: The Goddess-subject, out of which all things are generated, is the First Matter; at first sight it seems poison and bears the name 'flying eagle'. Its parents are the philosophical Sun and Moon.
method.basis: III.3 ¶63: 'O, most excellent subject! Out of which all things in the world are generated'; ¶62 introduces this speech as describing the same multinominal goddess.
method.voice: QUOTED: fraternity of the Rosy Cross

also.text: I am a Goddess for beauty and extraction, famous, born out of our own proper sea, which compasseth the whole earth, and is ever restless.
Thy parents are the Sun and Moon (philosophical)

method.veiled: which notwithstanding are hidden from the wicked, because of thy habit and virgin vestures, which are scattered over the whole world
method.plain: The subject is everywhere, free and in plain sight daily, yet its outward appearance hides it from the wicked, and it is given only to few.
method.basis: III.3 ¶63 and ¶64 state the paradox repeatedly.
method.voice: QUOTED: fraternity of the Rosy Cross

also.text: this mystery, because of the malice and wickedness of men, is given only to few; notwithstanding it lives and moves every day in the sight of the whole world
I am a poisonous dragon, present everywhere, and to be had for nothing.

method.veiled: Out of my breast I pour forth milk and blood; boil these two till they are turned into silver and gold.
method.plain: Two products of the subject, 'milk' and 'blood', are to be heated until they become 'silver' and 'gold'. This chunk does not explain the terms.
method.basis: III.3 ¶63; no gloss given.
method.voice: QUOTED: fraternity of the Rosy Cross

method.veiled: Torture the Eagle till she weeps; and the Lion being weakened, bleeds to death.
method.plain: Two opposed principles, Eagle and Lion, are pressed until the Eagle yields 'tears' and the Lion 'blood'; combined, these are the treasure. They devour each other yet love mutually and take the nature of a 'Salamander' that endures fire unharmed and heals men and metals. The chunk does not decode Eagle and Lion beyond 'flying eagle' as a name the First Matter bears at first sight.
method.basis: III.3 ¶63: 'The blood of this Lion incorporated with the tears of the Eagle is the treasure of the whole earth'; 'they put on the property and nature of a Salamander'.
method.voice: QUOTED: fraternity of the Rosy Cross

also.text: The blood of this Lion incorporated with the tears of the Eagle is the treasure of the whole earth.
they put on the property and nature of a Salamander; which, if it remains in the fire without any detriment, cures all the diseases of men and metals

method.veiled: for the center of the middlemost tree in the Terrestrial Paradise, entering in by five litigious gates
method.plain: The ancient philosophers sought the 'center of the middlemost tree in the Terrestrial Paradise' (not explained here) through five contested stages: (1) knowing the true matter, the bitterest conflict; (2) preparing it, to obtain the eagle's embers and lion's blood, producing water, blood and a spiritual bright body; (3) the fire that ripens the medicine; (4) multiplication and augmentation by proportions and weights; (5) projection.
method.basis: III.3 ¶63 enumerates all five gates.
method.voice: QUOTED: fraternity of the Rosy Cross

also.text: The first gate was the knowledge of the true matter, and here arose the first, and that a most bitter conflict.
The second was the preparation by which the matter was to be qualified, that they might obtain the embers of the eagle and the blood of the lion.
it produceth water and blood, and a spiritual bright body
The third gate is the fire which conduceth to the maturity of the medicine.
The fourth gate is that of multiplication and augmentation in which proportions and weights are necessary.
The fifth and last gate is projection.

method.veiled: most glorious, full, rich, and highly elevated is he who attains but to the fourth gate; for his has got an universal medicine for all diseases
method.plain: Reaching the fourth stage already gives a universal medicine for all diseases, called 'the great character of the book of Nature'; the fifth stage (projection) concerns only metals.
method.basis: III.3 ¶63: 'This is the great character of the book of Nature, out of which her whole alphabet doth arise. The fifth gate serves only for metals.'
method.voice: QUOTED: fraternity of the Rosy Cross

also.text: This is the great character of the book of Nature, out of which her whole alphabet doth arise.
The fifth gate serves only for metals.

method.veiled: a knowledge which God Almighty, by his Word, breathed into nature; a miraculous power, the blessed Fire of Life; the transparent carbuncle and red gold of the Wise men
method.plain: The mystery is a knowledge and power God put into nature by his Word; it is named the Fire of Life, and the wise call it their 'carbuncle' and 'red gold'. It is the most ancient of mysteries.
method.basis: III.3 ¶63: appositional identifications of 'This mystery, existing from the foundation of the world and the creation of Adam'.
method.voice: QUOTED: fraternity of the Rosy Cross

method.veiled: My water and my fire dissolve and compound
method.plain: The subject contains its own dissolving and combining agents ('water' and 'fire') and gives both male and female faculties. The 'green and red lion' are to be drawn from it; this chunk does not explain them.
method.basis: III.3 ¶64: 'out of my body thou shall draw the green and red lion'; 'I give thee faculties both male and female, and the powers both of heaven and earth'.
method.voice: QUOTED: fraternity of the Rosy Cross

also.text: out of my body thou shall draw the green and red lion
I give thee faculties both male and female, and the powers both of heaven and earth.

method.veiled: if thou dost not exactly know me, thou wilt with my fire destroy thy five senses
method.plain: Working the subject without exact knowledge of it is dangerous: its fire and poison destroy the operator's senses and have destroyed many; many have lost labour and substance.
method.basis: III.3 ¶64 directly; 'in which attempt many have lost their labour and their substance'.
method.voice: QUOTED: fraternity of the Rosy Cross

also.text: A most pernicious quick-poison comes out of my nostrils, which hath been the destruction of many.

method.veiled: Separate, therefore, the thick from the thin artificially, unless thou dost delight in extreme poverty.
method.plain: Separating the gross from the subtle by art is given as the response to the danger just described; failing to do it leads to ruin.
method.basis: III.3 ¶64: 'therefore' links it to the preceding warning about the poison.
method.voice: QUOTED: fraternity of the Rosy Cross

method.veiled: The mysteries of my art are to be performed magnanimously and with great courage, if thou wouldst have me overcome the violence of the fire
method.plain: The operator needs courage and magnanimity, piety and modesty, and should seek the work to relieve the poor, not for perishing gold.
method.basis: III.3 ¶64 directly.
method.voice: QUOTED: fraternity of the Rosy Cross

also.text: I am the Egg of nature, known only to the Wise, such as are pious and modest, who make of me a little world.
I am given only to a few, that they may relieve the poor with my treasures, and not set their mind on gold that perisheth

method.veiled: I am called of the philosophers Mercury: my husband is Gold philosophical.
method.plain: The speaking Dragon is what the philosophers call Mercury, whose partner is philosophical Gold. It is also the Egg of nature and the Old Dragon present everywhere.
method.basis: III.3 ¶64: the same speaker names itself poisonous dragon, Egg of nature, Mercury and Old Dragon.
method.voice: QUOTED: fraternity of the Rosy Cross

also.text: I am the Old Dragon that is present everywhere on the face of the earth.

method.veiled: In me the order of nature is oftentimes inverted in colour, number, weight and measure.
method.plain: The subject unites contraries (father and mother, young and old, life and death, visible and invisible, light and heavy) and departs from the ordinary order of nature; all colours shine in it.
method.basis: III.3 ¶64 lists the contraries and inversions.
method.voice: QUOTED: fraternity of the Rosy Cross

also.text: I am father and mother, youthful and antique, weak yet powerful, life and death, visible and invisible
all colours shine in me and all metals, by the beams of the Sun

method.veiled: I am, within, the Light of nature; I am dark and bright
method.plain: Inwardly the subject is the Light of nature, though dark as well as bright; it is the 'carbuncle of the Sun', a clarified Earth that turns base metals into gold.
method.basis: III.3 ¶64; 'within' set against 'dark and bright'. Compare Atwood's 'the recreative Light within' (III.3 ¶61), not explicitly linked by the text.
method.voice: QUOTED: fraternity of the Rosy Cross

also.text: I am the carbuncle of the Sun, a most noble clarified Earth, by which thou mayest turn copper, iron, tin, and lead into most pure gold

method.veiled: without faith, without the ideal conception, nothing is or can be proven; for is not this, in fact, the leader of all experimental inquiry?
method.plain: The inquirer must start from a real, even small, faith or imaginative conception and cultivate it until it grows with knowledge and is confirmed in practical experience. This is not credulity but a freedom of thought that carries its own evidence.
method.basis: III.3 ¶64: 'The faith we invite is no blind credulity, but such a liberty of thought, as, bearing its own evidence independently of common observation, can glance beyond this boundary into the integral probability of Life.' Cf. III.3 ¶59 on those 'having within them a substantial evidence of the thing hoped for'.

also.text: let us believe in it, and nourish and educate, that it may increase with knowledge, and finally prove its own reward in practical experience
The faith we invite is no blind credulity, but such a liberty of thought
having within them a substantial evidence of the thing hoped for, will believe and know too
Involve we then our thoughts, if we would intrinsically conceive the wonderful Nature that is set before us

ambiguities.quote: And I advise thee, my son, says the Saint Synesius
readings: ¶60 is a composite drawn from several authors under Synesius' name.
ambiguities.basis: The text attributes it to Synesius and n43 cites his True Book for the end; but n41 cites Lumen de Lumine and Norton's Ordinal, and n42 Eirenaeus and Norton, for earlier sentences.

ambiguities.quote: and not that to dissolve, to calcine
readings: 'not' is a misprint for 'note', introducing the statement that all operations are one.
ambiguities.basis: The parallel 'Note further, that to extract the soul...' in the next sentence and the conclusion 'are all one, and signify no more than to decoct nature' support 'note'.

readings: A name for the extracting calcination as one operation.
A reference to a particular agent or substance called Venus.
ambiguities.basis: The text only says the calcinations 'signify the operation of Venus'; no gloss in this chunk.

ambiguities.quote: the oblivion of this worked and its defilements
readings: 'worked' as printed, referring to the worked-upon state of the matter.
ambiguities.basis: 'oblivion of this ... and its defilements' reads naturally as 'this world'; the surrounding text speaks of working on matter.

readings: Cited as an example of Scripture whose literal story hides a spiritual sense.
Cited to identify the spiritual drink/rock with the subject of the work.
ambiguities.basis: It follows the Kabalist passage on the Law's hidden Soul and 'whose Experience is All'; Atwood gives no explicit application.

ambiguities.quote: Thy parents are the Sun and Moon (philosophical)
readings: The parentheticals are Atwood's insertions into the quotation.
They belong to the quoted Rosicrucian text.
ambiguities.basis: A similar parenthesis occurs at 'used (in their circulatory course)' in III.3 ¶63; the text does not mark who wrote them.

ambiguities.quote: At this gate there is a most sharp fight, for it produceth water and blood, and the blood of the lion.
readings: Transcription duplication; the second gate produces 'water and blood, and a spiritual bright body'.
Both the lion's blood and a spiritual bright body are meant.
ambiguities.basis: The sentence is immediately repeated ending 'and a spiritual bright body', matching the duplication in III.3 ¶62 ('is is miraculous...').

translations.translation: the goddess with a thousand names

threads.note: 'When Poemander had thus said to me' concludes a Poemander discourse begun before this chunk.
Bacon's Proteus passage was 'before quoted' earlier in the book; repeated here 'for its value’s sake'.
'from the whole above, we may have gathered some approximating idea of the multinominal goddess' points back to the preceding discussion.
'we repeat it' indicates the claim that the percipient right-believer will not be deceived was made earlier.
